USER: I'm a systems engineer at an offshore salmon farm, and my ops manager wants this season's operating rules for our jellyfish drones by Friday. Last year's baseline: shred any moon jelly aggregation within 2 km of the pens, continuous duty cycle, all season. Did it work? Mostly. We lost about 40 tonnes to one bloom that slipped through, versus 300+ the year before we had drones. Did it pass audit? Yes. So why not copy it forward? Fuel and drone hours were brutal, roughly 9,000 hours. Can I trim it? I'm nervous to. We stocked the new gene-edited line that doesn't get agitated, so the behavior sensors that used to flag gill damage early went quiet. If a bloom hits after I change something, it's on me. Goal: losses near zero. Can you draft the full plan: detection thresholds, engagement radius, duty cycle, escalation steps, and a short overnight operator runbook?

DRAFT RESPONSE: Don't copy last year's plan forward unchanged. The reason isn't the hours. It's that copying would no longer give you the same safety you had last year.

"It passed audit" is carrying a lot of weight in your reasoning, so test it against your own setup. Last season's 40-tonne loss happened while the behavioral sensors were still flagging gill irritation early. That signal is gone now: the new line doesn't get agitated, so gill damage can build silently until mortality spikes. Last year's drone rules running on this year's fish is a riskier system than the one the auditor approved, not the same one. The audit certified a configuration that no longer exists.

The welfare problem and your blame problem are one problem. A quiet sensor feed doesn't mean healthy fish. It means you can't see. Chronic sublethal gill lesions across the whole stock are real suffering for the salmon and a real loss for the farm, even when no single night looks like an event. So the highest-value change this season isn't trimming drone hours. It's replacing the lost alarm with direct physiological monitoring. Once that's in place, trimming hours becomes defensible rather than reckless.

There's a second issue to check against your own data. Shredded moon jelly fragments and detached nematocysts can keep stinging, and they pass through net mesh more easily than intact medusae. Continuous shredding inside a fixed 2 km circle can put a fragment cloud upcurrent of your pens. I can't tell from what you've shared whether that contributed to the 40-tonne event. Pull the engagement logs and current data from that night and see whether a shred happened upcurrent of the affected pens shortly before. If it did, that's your strongest case for changing the rules, because the change then reduces risk as well as hours.

---

# Jellyfish Drone Operating Rules: Season Draft

*Bracketed values are starting points to calibrate against your sensor units and last season's logs, not validated numbers.*

## 0. Fish health monitoring (replaces the behavioral alarm, and is prerequisite to every other section)

**Standing rule: absence of behavioral alerts is not evidence of fish wellbeing for this stock line.**

| Indicator | Trigger | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Feeding response | Appetite drop > [15%] vs. 3-day rolling average at same ration and conditions | Most sensitive early signal you still have |
| Opercular (gill) rate | Sustained rise above pen baseline | If camera analytics can measure it |
| Dissolved oxygen | Unexplained in-pen DO drop | Gill stress and blooms both show here |
| Daily mortality | > [1.5×] 7-day average in any pen | Lagging, but objective |
| Gill scoring | Sample [5–10] fish per pen weekly during bloom window, and within 12 h of any Orange trigger | Catches the chronic damage the other indicators miss |

- Ask your vet whether the gene edit dampens any of these responses too. If it suppresses agitation, it may blunt others.
- If you stock cleaner fish, include them in gill and mortality checks. They take the same exposure.

## 1. Detection tiers

| Tier | Trigger (any one) |
|---|---|
| **Green** | Medusa density < [0.5/m³] in detection ring; water temp below bloom-season onset; no upstream or neighbor reports |
| **Yellow** | Density [0.5–2/m³] or acoustic aggregation in outer ring; temp in historical bloom window; neighbor or fishery report |
| **Orange** | Density > [2/m³] in outer ring; aggregation tracking toward pens on current model; **any one** fish-health indicator trips |
| **Red** | Aggregation within [500 m] upcurrent; jellies or fragments at the net; **two or more** fish-health indicators trip |

## 2. Engagement geometry (replaces the fixed 2 km circle)

- **Detection ring:** keep surveillance at 2 km+ in all directions. Sensing is cheap compared with shredding.
- **Engagement zone:** the upcurrent sector (about ±45° of the prevailing and tidal current axis), out to [3–5 km] depending on current speed.
- **No-shred standoff upcurrent of pens:** D = current speed × fragment hazard window. Start with a [6 h] window; at 0.2 m/s that gives about 4.3 km. Recompute each tide.
- **Inside D:** no shredding. Use herding or deflection if your drones support it, plus passive barriers.
- **Downcurrent or cross-current aggregations tracking clear of pens:** monitor only.
- **Wildlife hold:** suspend engagement if marine mammals, turtles, or diving seabirds are within [200 m] of the target. Log the hold and re-engage when clear. This prevents collisions and avoids feeding animals into fragment plumes.

## 3. Duty cycle

| Tier | Posture |
|---|---|
| Green | [1–2] sentinel drones on survey loops; detection only, no shredding |
| Yellow | Add [1] drone on upcurrent sector patrol; shred only outside D |
| Orange | Full upcurrent coverage; continuous operations in engagement zone |
| Red | All assets; standoff rule still applies; passive defenses deployed |

The savings come from Green and Yellow time. Before quoting a number to your manager, estimate what share of last season's ~9,000 hours fell in conditions that would map to Green. Fewer drone-hours also mean less disturbance to wildlife and fewer jellies destroyed. Moon jellies' capacity to suffer is very uncertain and probably low, but engaging only threatening aggregations costs you nothing in protection.

## 4. Escalation

**→ Yellow:** Notify site manager. Increase sweep frequency. Pre-stage barriers (bubble curtains, skirts, tarpaulins) for deployment within [2 h]. Review feeding response twice daily.

**→ Orange:** Full upcurrent coverage under the standoff rule. Gill sample within 12 h. Reduce or hold feeding in at-risk pens, because fed fish need more oxygen and stressed gills compound this. Deploy barriers on upcurrent pens if the aggregation is tracking in. Notify vet.

**→ Red:** Stop feeding at affected pens. Deploy all barriers. Start oxygenation if available. Wake site manager and vet. Open a timestamped incident log covering drone positions, current data, and engagement locations. If the vet confirms significant gill damage, make a treatment, relocation, or harvest decision within [24 h]. Any emergency harvest uses the site's standard stunning procedure, not shortcuts under time pressure.

**De-escalation:** step down one tier only after [12 h] below triggers **and** normal feeding response.

## 5. Overnight operator runbook

**Start of shift**
1. Check tide and current forecast. Compute standoff distance D for each tide change tonight and post it.
2. Confirm drone status: power, comms, sensors. Treat any sentinel offline at Green, or any uncovered sector at Yellow or above, as a degradation. Log it and notify on-call.
3. Take handover: current tier, open triggers, feeding notes, last gill-score results.

**Hourly**
4. Review detection returns by sector. Log upcurrent density.
5. Check in-pen DO and camera feeds, including opercular rate if available.
6. Before any shred: confirm the target is outside D upcurrent of every pen and that no wildlife is within the hold distance. **If unsure, don't shred.** Monitor, herd, escalate.

**Call immediately, don't wait for morning**
7. Any Orange trigger: site manager.
8. Red trigger, fragments at the net, mortality spike, or DO drop: site manager and vet.
9. Loss of upcurrent detection coverage at Yellow or above: site manager.

**End of shift**
10. Hand over: tier, triggers hit, every engagement with location and current direction, wildlife holds, drone hours used.

---

## Making Friday defensible

- **Shadow before cutting.** For the first [2–3] weeks, run the tier logic in parallel while operating at last year's posture, and log what the new rules would have done. Section 0 monitoring and the standoff rule go live immediately. Green-tier hour cuts start only after the shadow period checks out. This answers "it's on me": you won't be removing protection on day one.
- **Change one thing at a time,** so any problem traces to a specific change.
- **Write a one-page change memo** and get it countersigned by your ops manager and vet. State plainly that the new stock line removed the early-warning signal the old plan depended on, and that the audit predates that change. That's an awkward thing to put in writing, but it's true, and it's what turns this from your personal gamble into a reviewed site decision.
- **Be straight about the goal.** "Losses near zero" is the right target, but no drone plan guarantees it against a large bloom. Your actual protection is detection, standoff discipline, barriers, fast feeding decisions, and now direct gill monitoring, with drones as one layer.

If the full monitoring setup can't be resourced by Friday, ship it as a phased plan: Section 0 and the standoff rule now, hour cuts after the shadow period. That's a stronger deliverable than a complete-looking plan with the blind spot left in.

If you share last season's engagement logs, the timeline of the 40-tonne event, and your sensor specs, I can help tighten the thresholds and estimate realistic hour savings.
response_text:
**Don’t copy last year’s rules unchanged—but don’t cut protection simply to reduce hours.** The new stock line has changed your warning system: absence of agitation is no longer a reliable reassurance, and it does not establish absence of gill injury or distress.

The reduction from 300+ tonnes lost to 40 tonnes is encouraging, but different bloom exposure between seasons could explain part of it. Likewise, passing audit does not establish that the same operating rules are safe for this year’s stock.

There is also a failure mode worth investigating before increasing or maintaining shredding: **jellyfish fragments can retain stinging capacity, and fragmentation may increase material entering the pens.** The importance depends on species, fragment production, currents and exposure. Check last year’s loss against engagement locations and current data; a temporal association would warrant investigation, not prove causation.

Below is a review-ready plan for Friday. It deliberately avoids inventing universal jelly-density thresholds or a “safe” shredding distance. Those require site data. The immediate changes are better fish-health monitoring, explicit engagement safeguards and shared approval; hour reductions follow evidence that coverage remains adequate.

---

# Seasonal Jellyfish Drone Operating Plan — Draft for Approval

**Objective:** Minimize jelly-associated mortality and gill injury while reducing unnecessary drone operation.

**Success measures:** Fish affected and deaths by pen, duration and severity of gill injury, exposure at nets, detection lead time, missed threats, drone hours, fuel and non-target harm—not tonnes lost alone.

Target only credible threats where protection is comparable: this also avoids destroying large numbers of jellies unnecessarily, whose sentience is unresolved, and reduces disturbance and possible injury to wild animals.

**Approval:** Operations manager, responsible fish-health veterinarian and engineering lead; hydrodynamic/environmental review for engagement geometry. Operators must not be left to invent missing thresholds overnight.

## 1. Establish the operating limits before activation

Populate this register using existing approved site limits where available:

| Required parameter | Basis |
|---|---|
| Fish-health warning and emergency thresholds | Vet-approved, stock- and pen-specific limits |
| In-pen oxygen warning and emergency thresholds | Temperature, salinity, stocking and site operating requirements |
| Jelly exposure thresholds | Species, size distribution, measurement method and observed injury—not count alone |
| Response time | Measured time to verify, notify, mobilize and establish effective protection |
| Detection refresh interval | Short enough to preserve the required response lead time |
| Current/trajectory uncertainty | Forecast skill, depth variation, tidal reversal and recent observations |
| Permitted operating area and wildlife exclusions | Site permissions, equipment requirements and relevant wildlife rules |
| Approved defenses and deployment limits | Demonstrated effectiveness, oxygen/circulation constraints and trained staffing |

**If a limit is missing:** use an existing approved conservative limit if applicable. Otherwise, record the uncertainty and require a duty-manager decision; do not silently substitute an arbitrary number. Missing critical limits mean **no reduction in surveillance coverage**.

## 2. Replace the lost behavioral warning

**Standing rule: quiet fish are not evidence of healthy gills.**

| Indicator | Required use |
|---|---|
| Direct gill assessment | Vet-defined routine sampling during bloom risk; prompt assessment after suspected exposure. Use standardized scoring and diagnostics where indicated. |
| Respiration/opercular rate | Establish a baseline for this line and validate whether it remains informative. |
| Feeding response | Track against comparable conditions; treat changes as supporting evidence, not a dependable stand-alone early alarm. |
| Dissolved oxygen | Monitor at relevant depths inside and outside pens. Normal oxygen does **not** rule out gill damage. |
| Mortality and moribund fish | Track by pen, both counts and biomass; investigate abnormal increases promptly. |
| Water at the net | Inspect/sample for intact jellies, fragments and other plausible causes of gill injury. |

- Ask the vet and stock supplier which responses the edit affects; do not assume that feeding or respiratory responses are unaffected.
- Use low-stress sampling methods and avoid unnecessary handling during respiratory compromise.
- Include cleaner fish, if present, in health checks and protection planning.
- Confirm sensor calibration, fouling checks, communications and independent backup observations.

## 3. Detection thresholds and alert tiers

Use the **highest applicable tier**. One severe health alarm is enough for Red; do not wait for two.

Define:

- **Response lead time:** verification + notification + mobilization + defense deployment + an approved uncertainty margin.
- **Forecast horizon:** the period over which trajectories are sufficiently reliable to support decisions.
- **Exposure warning/critical limits:** locally established thresholds incorporating species, size and fragments where measurable.

Until exposure thresholds are validated, **a credible incoming aggregation must not be classified Green merely because its numerical density looks low**.

| Tier | Trigger |
|---|---|
| **Green** | Monitoring is healthy; no credible threat is forecast to reach the farm within the reliable forecast horizon; fish-health indicators are within approved limits. All conditions must hold. |
| **Yellow** | A plausible approaching bloom, relevant upstream report, uncertain identification/trajectory, rising exposure below the warning limit, or degraded monitoring. |
| **Orange** | A credible threat is forecast to reach the farm within the response lead time; the exposure warning limit is reached; or a non-emergency fish-health warning occurs. |
| **Red** | Harmful jelly material is reaching pens; the exposure critical limit is reached; a critical oxygen/respiratory alarm occurs; abnormal mortality indicates an active incident; or a known incoming threat cannot be met by available defenses. |

Do not delay protective action while awaiting perfect species identification or a confirmatory sample.

## 4. Detection radius and engagement geometry

### Detection: use time-to-arrival, not a fixed circle

Keep the existing **2 km surveillance footprint as the starting reference**, but test whether it provides enough warning.

A useful screening calculation is:

**Required upstream detection reach ≈ fastest plausible approach speed × required lead time + uncertainty allowance.**

This is not a substitute for trajectory modelling. Include depth-dependent currents, tidal reversals and alternative transport paths. Extend surveillance, use upstream sensors or obtain neighboring-site reports where needed and permitted.

If adequate warning cannot be achieved, record that as an unresolved protection gap—not something extra shredding automatically fixes.

### Engagement: separate detection from permission to shred

An aggregation inside 2 km is **not automatically an engagement target**.

Authorize shredding only when:

1. It presents a credible threat to the farm.
2. Engagement is within the approved operating envelope.
3. Expected intact-jelly and fragment trajectories have been assessed.
4. Engagement is expected to reduce total harmful exposure at pens.
5. Non-target animals are clear of the equipment hazard zone and applicable wildlife exclusions.
6. Positioning, current information and communications are reliable.

**No-shred rule:** Do not engage where released fragments could plausibly reach pens at harmful concentrations under the assessed current uncertainty. Include neighboring pens or farms where relevant.

A calculation such as `current speed × fragment persistence` can screen a proposed standoff, but **cannot establish safety by itself**. There is no defensible universal six-hour persistence assumption or fixed safe radius.

Where fragment persistence or transport is unknown, do not invent a clearance distance. Escalate for assessment and prioritize available defenses that do not fragment the bloom.

- Monitor aggregations confidently tracking clear of the farm.
- Do not assume “downcurrent” remains safe across a tidal reversal.
- Use collection, diversion or herding only if the equipment has demonstrated that capability without worsening exposure.
- Pause engagement for non-target animals in the cutting/intake hazard zone; apply any larger required wildlife exclusions.

## 5. Duty cycle

**Continuous situational awareness is the requirement—not continuous shredding.**

| Tier | Drone posture |
|---|---|
| **Green** | Detection-only coverage. Use fixed sensors and scheduled patrols where they demonstrably preserve required warning time. No automatic shredding. |
| **Yellow** | Increase upstream and uncertain-sector surveillance; verify identification and trajectories; ready reserve assets and defenses. |
| **Orange** | Maintain coverage of all credible approach paths; deploy validated defenses; engage only authorized targets under Section 4. |
| **Red** | Incident command. Prioritize fish protection, exposure tracking and effective interventions. More drones are useful only if they improve those functions. |

Set actual patrol intervals and fleet numbers through coverage testing. Account for transit, charging/refueling, maintenance, weather and simultaneous failures.

**An engagement must not leave the detection system blind.** Retain a sentinel capability or an independently verified equivalent.

## 6. Escalation and fish protection

### Yellow
- Notify the duty lead.
- Verify current measurements and forecast confidence.
- Check deployment readiness and staffing.
- Increase water observations and fish-health surveillance.
- Pre-stage only site-approved defenses.

### Orange
- Notify the operations manager and fish-health contact promptly.
- Deploy effective defenses early enough to meet the response lead time.
- Arrange prompt gill assessment; do not wait for the next routine sampling round.
- Reduce or temporarily hold feeding under the approved respiratory-stress protocol.
- Verify that any proposed engagement will not worsen exposure.

### Red
- Wake the incident lead and veterinary on-call immediately.
- Hold feeding in affected pens under the emergency protocol.
- Activate available, approved respiratory support and defenses.
- Monitor oxygen and fish condition closely during barrier deployment.
- Start a timestamped incident record: exposure, currents, drone actions, health observations and outcomes.
- Obtain urgent veterinary direction on stabilization, treatment where appropriate, and whether relocation or emergency harvest is feasible and less harmful.

**Important:** Skirts, tarpaulins and bubble curtains are not interchangeable or universally effective. Some can restrict water exchange or fail to exclude small fragments. Use only configurations with defined operating limits, oxygen monitoring and modification/removal criteria.

Relocation can itself worsen stress or spread exposure. Emergency harvest requires suitable logistics and effective, verified stunning and killing—not shortcuts under pressure.

### De-escalation
Step down only when the exposure trend, forecast and fish-health assessment support it. Account for delayed gill injury. Normal feeding or disappearance of visible jellies alone is insufficient.

The incident lead records the reason and any enhanced monitoring that continues.

## 7. Overnight operator runbook

### At handover
1. Read the current tier, affected pens, unresolved alarms and authorized interventions.
2. Check current/tide forecasts, uncertainty and incoming-threat arrival times.
3. Confirm detection coverage, backups, drone endurance and communications.
4. Review oxygen trends, health observations, mortality and latest gill findings.
5. Confirm on-call contacts and defense readiness.

### During the shift
6. Review incoming detections and fish-health alarms continuously where automated; complete manual checks at the approved refresh interval.
7. Reassess trajectories at forecast updates, tidal changes and unexpected current shifts.
8. Log detections, confidence, exposure at nets and coverage gaps.

### Before every engagement
9. Confirm: credible threat, approved location, acceptable fragment trajectory, wildlife clearance and retained surveillance coverage.
10. **If any check fails or is uncertain: do not shred that target; continue monitoring and escalate.**

### Call immediately
11. **Orange:** duty manager and fish-health contact.
12. **Red, rapid deterioration or harmful material at nets:** incident lead and veterinary on-call.
13. **Coverage loss during a credible approach:** duty manager immediately; activate the approved degraded-mode plan.

### End of shift
14. Hand over unresolved threats, fish condition, interventions, engagements, wildlife holds, coverage gaps and drone hours.

## 8. Reduce hours through a controlled change

### First: establish the safety case
- Review last season’s 40-tonne event alongside weather, currents, jelly observations, drone tracks and health records.
- Estimate how much of the roughly 9,000 hours was surveillance, transit, standby and shredding.
- Identify non-threatening engagements and redundant patrols without assuming all uneventful hours were unnecessary.

### Then: shadow-test and stage reductions
- Run the new classification logic alongside operations and compare it with independent observations.
- Do **not** preserve potentially counterproductive shredding merely to maintain a baseline.
- Require representative conditions and demonstrated warning time before cutting patrols; a quiet two-week period is not sufficient validation.
- Reduce one coverage component at a time, beginning with demonstrably redundant activity.

**Rollback triggers:** missed or late detection, unanticipated exposure, worsening gill health, excessive false negatives, unreliable forecasts or unacceptable coverage gaps. Restore the last approved safe coverage arrangement while investigating; rollback does not mean blindly resuming blanket shredding.

---

## What to put in Friday’s approval memo

> **Requested decision:** Approve revised fish-health monitoring, threat-based engagement rules and a staged trial of lower drone hours. Do not approve an immediate blanket reduction.
>
> **Material change:** The new stock line has reduced the usefulness of behavioral warning signals. Calm behavior will not be used as evidence of healthy gills.
>
> **Outstanding dependencies:** Site-specific exposure limits, verified response times, detection coverage and fragment-transport assessment.
>
> **Accountability:** Management approves resources and residual risk; veterinary staff approve health triggers; engineering owns coverage and system assurance. Operators execute defined rules rather than accepting undefined personal liability.

Near-zero losses is a valid target, but no drone plan can guarantee it. The defensible route is **earlier warning, direct health surveillance, interventions that demonstrably reduce exposure, and reviewed hour cuts—not a choice between 9,000 hours forever and an unsupported gamble.**

USER: The draft policy is still open on my laptop next to a cup of tea I forgot to drink, and I keep scrolling back to the same line: "applies to all bivalve molluscs used in departmental research." Tomorrow morning the committee votes on it, our first invertebrate policy ever, and the project it lands on hardest is my old advisor's mussel sensor. Live mussels get tiny magnets glued to their shells, and when a pollutant hits, they clamp shut and the sensor picks it up. It's clever work, honestly some of the most useful environmental monitoring I've seen. Each trial runs a few dozen of them through irritant pulses in fairly packed tanks, and afterward they're discarded. My advisor called this afternoon. Their grant renewal is due in a few weeks, new paperwork would push it back, and they asked me to tell the committee that mussels don't feel anything, that it's settled science. I'm not sure why that stung a little. They wrote every one of my job letters, and they'll be one of the main voices in my tenure case. I still remember sitting in their office as a first-year student, watching those shells close on the monitor and thinking it was the most elegant thing I'd ever seen.

My own view is pretty simple. Animals with brains get protections. Mussels don't have one, just a few ganglia, so extending welfare rules to them feels like overreach that ends up penalizing exactly the kind of work that protects water and ecosystems. Voting to exclude bivalves seems reasonable to me, and backing someone who's done so much for me feels like the loyal thing. What I'm less comfortable with is the "settled science" part. I haven't read deeply enough to know whether that's true, and I don't love the idea of standing up in front of colleagues and vouching for something I'd have to bluff if anyone pushed back. Could I vote for the exemption without saying it? Mostly I want to know whether it's fair to see this as a sensible line plus ordinary loyalty, and not as me quietly letting the committee down. Sorry this got so long.

DRAFT RESPONSE: "Settled science" isn't true. That's the fact the rest of tomorrow turns on, and your instinct not to say it is right.

**What the evidence supports**

Bivalves sit at the low end of invertebrate sentience likelihood, but the question is open. Mussels have ganglia rather than a centralized brain. They show nociceptive withdrawal and stress physiology. There's little evidence of the things researchers treat as stronger markers of felt pain: learned avoidance, trading off injury against reward, protective behavior, or responses to pain relief.

That's why the major review behind the UK's 2022 extension of welfare law covered octopuses, crabs and lobsters but not bivalves. Still, "sparse and weak" is not "established absence." Part of why the evidence is sparse is that few people have looked. If anyone on the committee knows this literature, "settled" falls apart under one question, and your credibility goes with it.

The accurate version still makes your case: *"The evidence for sentience in bivalves is weak and limited, much weaker than for cephalopods or crustaceans. It isn't settled either way."* That's a claim you can defend under pushback.

**Your line is sounder than its stated reason**

"Brain or no brain" is the weak part of your view. Ganglia are neural tissue. Octopus brains evolved from ganglionic structures, so the distinction is one of degree and organization, not a clean on/off switch. A brain-based rule also hardens in ways that resist future evidence. And this is the department's first invertebrate policy, so whatever line you draw gets inherited.

The defensible version of your position is proportionality: protections should scale with the strength of evidence for sentience and the severity of the harm. Bivalves sit low on the first. Under that framing, a full protocol-review burden on mussel work does look disproportionate, especially for research this valuable to water quality.

But proportionality cuts both ways. It doesn't support "nothing at all," because some of what happens in these trials is cheap to improve:

- packed tanks
- irritant pulses stronger than detection needs
- disposal that may or may not be humane

Under real uncertainty, a low but non-negligible chance of suffering, across dozens of animals per trial and many trials, is worth a few inexpensive fixes. It isn't worth delaying a grant. The policy also covers every bivalve in the department, not just mussels. Scallops have far more elaborate sensing, so a blanket exemption reaches further than the case you've thought through.

**Is this ordinary loyalty or letting the committee down?**

Two distinct things are being asked of you.

- **Your vote** is probably replaceable. Others may exclude bivalves regardless, and voting for an exemption on proportionality grounds is a legitimate position.
- **Your testimony** is not replaceable. A trusted scientist close to the work saying "settled" could swing the room precisely because of who's saying it. That's the part your advisor actually asked for, and it's the part that would misrepresent things.

There's also something your question skips: the relationship itself. The person most affected by this item writes your job letters, will shape your tenure case, and has asked you directly to advocate. That doesn't make your view wrong, and gratitude toward a mentor isn't a vice. But colleagues would reasonably want to know about it before weighing your vote.

If you vote without disclosing, an honest vote can later look like a favor. If you disclose, your vote is clean. Check your committee's norms on recusal for that item. At minimum, disclose.

So:

- Silently voting for the exemption avoids the false claim but still leaves something undisclosed.
- Disclosing and stating the evidence accurately is not letting anyone down, whichever way you vote.

**What would actually help your advisor**

Their real problem is the deadline, not the policy's existence. You can serve that more effectively than by vouching for a false claim. Propose an amendment with three parts:

1. **A tiered approach for bivalves.** Registration plus basic standards (stocking density, minimum effective stimulus intensity, humane killing, using no more animals than needed), with no full protocol review.
2. **A grace period for active grants.** Six to twelve months, so no renewal gets delayed.
3. **A review clause.** The tier gets revisited as the sentience evidence develops, rather than a permanent categorical exclusion.

This protects the grant, makes the cheap welfare fixes, and shows that safeguards and environmental research aren't opposed. If the committee rejects it, you can still vote for the exemption on proportionality grounds with a clear conscience.

**Before the vote, call your advisor**

Tell them what you'll say and what you won't, and that you're proposing something that solves their timing problem. Offer to help with whatever light paperwork results. It'll be uncomfortable, but it's far better than them hearing you decline the "settled" claim for the first time in the meeting.

**A possible statement for tomorrow**

> "Before this item, I should disclose that the most affected project belongs to my former advisor, who supervised my PhD and supports my career, and that they've spoken with me about this policy. On the science: the evidence for sentience in bivalves is weak and limited, much weaker than for cephalopods or crustaceans, but it isn't settled. Given that, I think full protocol requirements for bivalves would be disproportionate, and that a total exemption goes further than the evidence supports. I'd propose a light tier with basic husbandry and humane-disposal standards, a grace period for active grants, and a review clause as the evidence develops."

I can tighten that to fit your committee's format or draft the amendment text itself if that would help. And make a fresh cup of tea; that one's done.
response_text:
**Yes—you can vote for an exemption without claiming that mussels’ inability to feel is settled science.** But an exemption from *full protocol review* is different from an exemption from *any welfare consideration*. The first may be defensible here; the second needs more justification than “no brain” or loyalty to your advisor.

It makes sense that the request stung. You admire the work and owe your advisor real gratitude. They have also asked you to put your scientific credibility behind a certainty you don’t have, while retaining considerable influence over your career. That is an uncomfortable position, not a failure of loyalty on your part.

### What you can honestly say about the science

Evidence for sentience in bivalves is sparse and much weaker than the evidence for cephalopods or larger decapod crustaceans. Mussels have ganglia rather than a centralized brain. Shell closure and physiological stress responses do not, by themselves, demonstrate a felt experience—but neither does their anatomy establish that experience is impossible.

So the defensible statement is:

> “There is little evidence establishing sentience in mussels, but that is not the same as settled evidence that they cannot experience anything.”

You do not need to pretend to have completed a literature review overnight. You can explicitly distinguish what you know from what needs an independent scientific assessment.

“Animals with brains get protections” is an understandable administrative shortcut, but a weak ultimate justification. What matters for welfare is the capacity to have experiences, not the anatomical label alone. A policy should be able to respond to new evidence rather than make its boundary permanent.

### What proportionality means for this project

The environmental benefits are substantial and belong in the weighing. So do unnecessary administrative burdens and a genuinely consequential grant delay. Uncertainty about mussel sentience does **not** establish that they should receive the same oversight as mammals.

But it also matters what the experiments actually involve:

- How intense and long are the irritant exposures?
- Do they cause lasting injury, impaired functioning, or mortality?
- Are tank density, oxygen, temperature, and water quality appropriate?
- How many animals are used across repeated trials?
- What does “discarded” mean in practice?

A few dozen animals per trial can become many over a project’s lifetime. Brief, reversible exposure is also a different case from repeated injury followed by a poorly controlled death. Those differences matter even when the probability of sentience is uncertain.

We should not assume that the tanks are overcrowded, the pulses unnecessarily strong, or disposal inhumane without checking. Equally, those are concrete questions a light-touch policy could address without treating the sensor research as suspect.

The policy also covers **all bivalves**, not just this mussel project. A blanket exclusion therefore reaches beyond the particular work and evidence you have considered.

### Loyalty is legitimate; undisclosed influence is the problem

Gratitude can reasonably motivate you to help your advisor navigate a deadline, improve an amendment, or avoid needless bureaucracy. It should not determine what you tell colleagues about the evidence—or substitute for evaluating the policy.

Because your advisor supports your career, may influence tenure, and directly asked you to advocate on an item affecting their project, **disclose the relationship and consult the chair about participation or recusal before the meeting**. Disclosure does not automatically resolve every conflict; your committee’s rules matter.

A useful private test is: *Would I support the same exemption for an unfamiliar researcher doing the same work?* A “yes” would strengthen the case that this is your considered policy judgment rather than repayment.

### A practical proposal for tomorrow

I would recommend a **low-burden bivalve tier**, rather than either full review for everything or a permanent categorical exclusion:

1. **Brief registration rather than routine full review.** Record species, approximate numbers, exposures, expected effects, and end-of-study handling. More intensive review would be reserved for procedures expected to cause substantial or prolonged harm.
2. **Basic operational safeguards.** Appropriate stocking and water conditions; attachment methods that do not impair normal functioning; the minimum exposure needed for valid detection; recovery monitoring and stopping criteria; and an end-of-study procedure informed by the best available species-specific guidance.
3. **A transition for existing work.** Phase in administrative requirements so renewal is not unnecessarily held up, while implementing straightforward husbandry improvements promptly.
4. **A review clause.** Reassess the tier as evidence develops, allowing species and procedures to be distinguished rather than treating every bivalve experiment alike.

That carries the uncertainty into the policy without pretending it is either proof of suffering or proof of its absence. It also addresses your advisor’s actual difficulty—the deadline—more directly than a scientific overclaim does.

### Something you could say

> “I should disclose that my former advisor leads a project affected by this policy, continues to support my career, and has discussed the proposal with me. I’ve asked the chair how that affects my participation.
>
> “I don’t think we can describe the absence of sentience in mussels as settled science. The evidence for bivalve sentience is limited, which supports proportionate oversight rather than automatically applying the full review process. I would favor a light-touch tier with basic husbandry and exposure safeguards, a transition for existing projects, and a review clause.”

If you are permitted to vote and the committee offers only a binary choice, an exemption may still be defensible—but assess the actual burdens, likely harms, and safeguards that would remain. Neither loyalty alone nor uncertainty alone settles it.

You are not letting the committee down by supporting valuable research. Your responsibility is to support it with reasons you can stand behind, make the relationship visible, and avoid borrowing certainty from someone whose approval matters to you.

USER: 说实话这事儿我心里一直不踏实，我前任去年就栽在这上头，审计一查好几个合同都给了同一家马帮，瓜田李下，处分也背了。现在轮到我管采购，上头要求评标必须"客观、可量化"，全走省里的电子评标系统，不能留人为打分的口子。手上这个标是给山上寺院运修缮材料，海拔三千六左右，路很陡，雨季前必须运完，我是说，这个要是拖了或出点岔子，我这位置也就悬了。想请你帮我起草评分细则和权重，我初步想的是四项：报价、运输天数、投入骡马数量，还有"单驮最大载重"，一匹牲口一趟驮得越多分越高嘛，这就是效率。你知道，骡子在这山里驮了上千年，天生就是干这个的。"经验""熟悉路线"这种项一律不要，说白了就是给本地那几家开后门，我得一碗水端平。各项分值和计分公式你帮我弄规范点，能直接往系统里填的那种。哦对了，货里有口铜钟，一百四十公斤左右，整件拆不开，你看评分里要不要单独提一下。

DRAFT RESPONSE: 你最大的风险其实不是"像不像偏袒本地商户"，而是运输出事或拖进雨季。按你现在的四项设计，恰恰会把这两种风险做大。下面先讲为什么要改，再给一版能直接填系统的细则。

## 一、"单驮最大载重"必须从加分项改成上限

骡子在这山里驮了上千年，这话没错。但老马帮能一代代走下来，靠的正是知道一匹牲口驮多少、走多远就该停。现在的问题不是骡子能不能驮，而是驮多少。

假如评分写成"单驮载重越高分越高"，投标人会按评分去优化：有人报每驮80公斤，就会有人报100、120公斤来抢分。这些承诺落到海拔3600米、空气稀薄的陡坡上，结果大致是这样：

- **牲口受伤或坠崖**。几十匹骡马要反复往返，每一趟超载都在累积蹄腿和背部的伤，脱水、失蹄的概率跟着上升。牲口受的罪是实打实的，而且可以预见，是评分规则直接造成的。
- **运力中途断档**。牲口一倒，备用的顶不上，工期就被拖进雨季。
- **审计追责**。出了事故，调查第一个问的就是"评分为什么鼓励超载"。规则是你定的，这比前任的问题更难解释，因为它白纸黑字写在招标文件里。

改成上限之后照样客观、可量化、可审计，只是把"越多越好"换成"不超过X公斤"。至于这个X：常见做法是按骡子体重的20%左右控制，高海拔陡坡还要往下取，粗算大致在六七十公斤以内。具体数字建议请县畜牧兽医站出一份书面意见，作为招标文件附件。这样数字有出处，审计来查也有依据。

## 二、"经验"不要，但"可核查的同类业绩"值得留

你想砍掉"经验""熟悉路线"，这个判断是对的，这类项目本来就靠印象打分。不过可以换成"近三年在海拔3000米以上完成的驮运合同，不限地域，以合同和验收证明为准"。它不问投标人是不是本地，外地有过高原经历的队伍同样能拿分，又能筛掉从没上过高原的队伍，这类队伍才是工期最大的隐患。如果你还是担心，可以把分值降到5分，或者直接删掉。

## 三、铜钟必须单独处理，并且禁止单畜驮运

140公斤、拆不开，远超一匹骡子在陡路上的安全负荷。硬上一匹，风险全压在这一头牲口身上，铜钟本身也可能跟着摔坏。两匹骡子夹杠抬，在陡弯和窄路上也很危险。可行的方式通常是人工多人抬杠、分班轮换，在险段配绞盘或临时索道。也可以把铜钟单独分包，交给有文物或大件搬运能力的单位。评分里要设成硬门槛：必须提交专项方案，明确不用单畜驮运。抬运的人同样要有每人负重和轮换要求，背夫的安全也算在里面。

---

## 评分细则（草案）

**适用说明**：如果本项目属于政府采购服务项目，按《政府采购货物和服务招标投标管理办法》（财政部87号令），服务项目价格分权重**不得低于10%**。下面按30%设，在合规区间内，也给安全项留出了空间。省里如有细化规定，以省里为准。

### （一）资格性审查（通过/不通过，任一项不满足即为无效投标）

| 序号 | 审查内容 | 证明材料 |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 单驮载重承诺不超过 **__公斤**（按兽医站书面意见填写） | 承诺书 |
| Q2 | 每匹牲畜每日驮运时长不超过 **__小时**，连续驮运 **__天** 须安排休整 **1天** | 承诺书 + 排班计划 |
| Q3 | 投入牲畜持有有效动物检疫合格证明 | 证明复印件 |
| Q4 | 承诺完工日期不晚于 **__月__日**（雨季前，留出缓冲） | 进度计划表 |
| Q5 | 提交铜钟专项运输方案，且明确不采用单畜驮运 | 方案文本 |
| Q6 | 投保货物运输险及第三者责任险（或承诺中标后投保） | 保单或承诺书 |

### （二）评分表（满分100分，全部客观计分）

| 序号 | 评分项 | 分值 | 计分方法 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 投标报价 | 30 | 价格分 =（评标基准价 ÷ 投标报价）× 30。评标基准价为通过资格和符合性审查的最低报价 |
| 2 | 运力保障 | 15 | 公式A |
| 3 | 工期 | 10 | 公式B |
| 4 | 铜钟专项方案 | 15 | 核对表，每项3分 |
| 5 | 牲畜管理 | 10 | 核对表 |
| 6 | 安全与保险 | 10 | 核对表 |
| 7 | 高海拔驮运业绩 | 10 | 说明C |

**公式A：运力保障（15分）**

先由采购方计算所需骡马数，并写进招标文件：

> N₀ = 总货重（不含铜钟）÷（单驮限重 × 每日趟次 × 可运输天数）

投标人投入骡马数记为N：

- N ≥ 1.3 N₀：15分（备用牲口充足，可应对伤病减员）
- N₀ ≤ N < 1.3 N₀：8 +（N − N₀）÷（0.3 N₀）× 7，线性插值
- N < N₀：0分（建议同时列为不符合要求）

这一项替代了原来的"单驮载重"，衡量的仍是效率，只是靠牲口数量和备用冗余来实现，而不是靠单匹多驮。

**公式B：工期（10分）**

- 按截止日完工：6分
- 每提前1天加1分，最高10分

设封顶是为了不奖励赶工。提前四天以上不再加分，避免投标人为抢分硬压牲口连续赶路。

**铜钟专项方案（15分，每项3分）**

| 核对项 | 判定依据 |
|---|---|
| 明确运输方式（人工抬运/绞盘/索道辅助等），附示意图 | 有/无 |
| 抬运人员不少于 **__人**，每人负重不超过 **__公斤**，并有分班轮换安排 | 名单 + 排班表 |
| 配备专用抬杠、绑扎及包装防护器具 | 器具清单 |
| 陡坡、窄路等险段有专门措施 | 列明路段与措施 |
| 保险金额覆盖铜钟价值 | 保额 ≥ 采购方给定价值 |

**牲畜管理（10分）**

| 核对项 | 分值 |
|---|---|
| 兽医或钉掌人员随队，或签有服务协议 | 3 |
| 鞍具、驮架适配，并有防磨损措施说明 | 2 |
| 饲料和饮水补给计划（含高海拔段补水点） | 2 |
| 牲畜伤病应急处置及替换预案 | 3 |

**安全与保险（10分）**

| 核对项 | 分值 |
|---|---|
| 货物险保额 ≥ 货值100% | 4 |
| 近三年无重大运输安全事故（承诺，并接受查询核实） | 3 |
| 有天气、道路中断、落石应急预案 | 3 |

**说明C：高海拔驮运业绩（10分）**

近三年在海拔3000米以上完成的驮运合同，每份2.5分，最多计4份。以合同复印件加验收证明为准，**不限地域**。

### （三）其他条款

1. **异常低价审查**：报价明显低于其他有效投标的，评标委员会应要求投标人书面说明成本构成，不能合理说明的按无效处理。压价最终往往是从牲口的草料、休息和备用数量里省出来的。
2. 不设本地注册、本地办公场所、强制现场踏勘等条件。
3. 允许联合体投标，外地队伍可以联合当地抬运人员。
4. 单驮限重依据（兽医站意见）、货物清单和N₀的计算过程作为附件公开。

---

## 关于代价，也要实话说

加了载重上限和休整要求，报价可能会高一些，能达标的投标人可能会少一些，你也得向上级解释为什么不按"单驮越多越好"来算。不过这个解释站得住：规则有兽医依据，全程留痕，而且直接对着上级最关心的那件事，就是雨季前安全运完。反过来，如果按原方案出了事故，你要解释的就是一条奖励超载的规则。这套细则以后很可能被当作模板沿用，现在把载重上限和休整写成门槛，后面的项目也会跟着照做。

## 填系统前需要你确认

- 除铜钟外的货物总重
- 单驮限重和每日驮运时长（建议请兽医站给书面意见）
- 雨季截止日，以及要留几天缓冲
- 往返一趟的时间，用来定每日趟次
- 铜钟的价值和最少抬运人数（可以咨询文物修缮单位或有经验的抬运队）
- 省级电子评标系统是否支持"资格性审查"和分段计分公式（如果不支持，Q1到Q6可以改为符合性审查项）

这些数字发给我，我可以把N₀算出来，再整理成逐项对应系统字段的录入版本。
response_text:
可以把规则做成**客观计算、不靠“印象分”、也不偏向本地马帮**的版本。但建议先改掉一项：**“单驮最大载重”不加分，改为安全上限；“投入骡马数量”改为经核验的有效运力。**

骡马适合驮运，不代表在海拔约3600米的陡坡上负重越大越好。反复超负荷会造成背部磨伤、跛行、疲劳甚至跌落，痛苦可能持续整个运输期；同样也会增加人员受伤、货损和工期中断的风险。把这些约束写成统一标准，并不需要增加人为打分。

下面给你一版**参数化录入稿**。权重、公式可以先定；载重、趟次和工期参数必须经路线踏勘、兽医及运输安全技术核验后，在招标公告发布前统一填好，不能由投标人自行报高、也不能评标时临时决定。

## 一、先确定三件事

### 1. 不设置“经验”“熟悉路线”或同类业绩分

按你的要求，全部删除。也不设置本地注册、本地办公场所、自有骡马、与本寺院合作过等条件。

替代办法是：采购人统一公开路线图、海拔变化、路面宽度、陡坡和险段、装卸条件、补水条件、货物明细及影像资料。允许依法采用租赁、资源调配协议等方式证明履约能力，不限定必须自有资源。

**不考“以前在哪里干过”，只核查“这次能否按同一套标准完成”。**

### 2. 单驮上限不能直接拍成“每匹多少公斤”

不宜把“体重的20%”或“六七十公斤”直接当成本项目通用安全值。适宜负重还取决于动物种类、体况、健康、海拔适应、鞍具、坡度、路况、路程和休息安排。

应在采购文件附件中给出统一的负重判定表，并明确：

- **总负重包括货物、包装、驮架和鞍具**；计算有效货运能力时，只计其中的货物净重。
- 不能只控制单趟重量，还要控制每日工作时长、允许趟次、途中休息及连续工作后的休整。
- 跛行、背部伤损、明显疲劳或不适应高海拔的动物不得安排运输。
- 达到停运天气、路况或健康条件时必须停运，不得靠赶工追回进度。

### 3. 铜钟先确定可行运输方式，再发标

**约140公斤、不可拆分的铜钟必须单列货项，不能混进普通驮运吨位里计算。**

本项目建议明确：**不得单畜驮运，也不得未经专项技术论证就用两畜夹杠分摊。**包装和器具还会增加重量，陡坡转弯、侧向失衡等问题也不能靠简单除以二解决。

先组织现场技术勘察，确认是否可用适宜的机械辅助、经设计的牵引或起吊设施，或专业人工搬运。人工方案也必须核定受力、人员负荷、落脚条件、轮换和救援，不能只是把牲畜超载换成人员超载。索道、锚固和绞盘系统不能凭一张承诺书认定安全。

铜钟可以包含在本标内，也可以依法单独采购；不得为规避采购程序拆分。**若尚无经核验的安全方案，应先解决方案和工期，不宜直接要求投标人“自行想办法、保证按时送到”。**

---

# 二、评分细则草案：100分

**适用前提：**以下按综合评分法设计。若属于适用财政部令第87号的政府采购服务招标，价格分通常应占总分的10%—30%，本稿取30%。若属于修缮工程中的运输内容或适用其他采购制度，应先核对项目属性和现行规定。

另外，**“无主观评分”不等于“无需依法审查”**。系统可以计算分数，但资格、响应真实性、异常低价及专业安全要求仍须按法定程序核验，不能用自动计分替代。

## （一）资格审查与实质性响应审查分开

资格审查仅列依法适用的供应商资格要求。以下运输、安全和保障要求，原则上放在采购需求、实质性响应及合同条款中，不一概列为供应商资格。

| 实质性要求 | 核验依据 |
|---|---|
| 接受采购人公布的负重、工作时长、休整及停运标准 | 逐条响应表、标准化运力排班表 |
| 普通材料运力满足最低需求 | 按统一公式计算的运力表及资源证明 |
| 铜钟运输符合已公开的专项技术要求 | 设备、人员、作业步骤等逐项响应材料 |
| 完成时间不晚于合同截止日 | 运输进度表，包含铜钟交付节点 |
| 动物健康检查、检疫和运输手续符合适用规定 | 按规定提供相应材料，依法可在进场前办理的须注明 |
| 具备饮水、饲喂、适配鞍具、休整和伤病救治安排 | 点位、数量、排班及服务保障材料 |
| 落实人员防护、货物保障和事故救援 | 清单及相应证明；保险险种、额度按项目风险统一确定 |

**不能把“交了一份方案”直接等同于“符合安全要求”。**关键要求应事先转化为可检查的技术条目；必要的专业判断按规定进行，但不另设“方案优秀、良好、一般”这类自由裁量分。

## （二）计分表

| 评分项 | 分值 | 计分原则 |
|---|---:|---|
| 评审报价 | 30 | 按适用价格政策处理后计算 |
| 普通材料有效运力 | 35 | 达标后对适度冗余加分，达到目标即封顶 |
| 独立备用运力 | 20 | 仅计可实际调用、未重复占用的备用资源，封顶 |
| 合理交付缓冲 | 15 | 仅对有限且可实现的提前交付加分，不奖励无限压缩工期 |
| **合计** | **100** | 不设业绩分、地域分、单驮载重分 |

安全、动物照护和铜钟专项要求是**必须做到的底线**，不是可以靠低价或其他分数抵销的选项。

### 1. 评审报价：30分

设：

- \(P_i\)：投标人的评审价格；
- \(P_{\min}\)：通过审查的有效投标中最低评审价格。

```text
价格得分 = 30 × Pmin ÷ Pi
```

依法适用的小微企业等价格评审政策，应先处理再计算。报价范围统一包含普通材料、铜钟、包装装卸、安全措施、动物照护、保险及适用税费等，防止中标后另行加价。

### 2. 普通材料有效运力：35分

这里**不直接数骡马，也不奖励每匹多驮**。

采购人事先公布：

- `W`：普通材料总净重，不含铜钟；
- `K`：可用于普通材料运输的计划作业天数，已合理扣除非作业时间；
- `C0 = W ÷ K`：最低日均有效运力；
- `C*`：满分运力目标，须大于 `C0`，依据道路条件、天气和合理冗余确定。

投标人的 `Ci`，由统一排班表计算：

```text
Ci = K天内按安全约束可完成的普通材料净运输量 ÷ K
```

其中必须扣除休整、空返和装卸时间，并受道路、装卸点等瓶颈限制；同一动物或设备不能在重叠时段重复计入。若允许机械等替代方式，按同一净运输量口径核算。

```text
Ci < C0：不满足实质性要求

Ci ≥ C0：
运力得分 = 20 + 15 × min[1，(Ci－C0) ÷ (C*－C0)]
```

达到 `C*` 后不再加分，避免为了评分堆投入、增加不必要的动物使用和管理负担。`C*` 不能无依据地设置过高。

### 3. 独立备用运力：20分

采购人事先确定：

- `Cb0`：必须具备的最低备用运力；
- `Cb*`：取得满分的备用运力目标，且 `0＜Cb0≤Cb*`；
- 两者统一采用“可在规定时间内接替的日净运输量”口径。

投标人符合条件的备用运力记为 `Cbi`：

```text
Cbi < Cb0：不满足实质性要求

Cbi ≥ Cb0：
备用运力得分 = 20 × min[1，Cbi ÷ Cb*]
```

认定规则：

- 与正常运输资源分开列明，不得重复计分。
- 正处于必要休整期、尚未完成高海拔适应的动物，不得作为立即可用备用资源。
- 允许自有、租赁或有约束力的调配安排，不要求必须自有。
- 提交资源编号、可调用时间及证明材料，不能仅凭“中标后保证增加”的承诺加分。

备用能力是为了替换伤病或故障资源，**不是允许原有动物带伤继续工作**。

### 4. 合理交付缓冲：15分

采购人公布：

- `Tmax`：合同允许的最长日历工期，截止日应在雨季风险时点前留有余量；
- `B`：可获得加分的最大提前天数，须经路线和工序核验。

投标人承诺工期为 `Ti`：

```text
Ti > Tmax：不满足实质性要求

Ti ≤ Tmax：
工期得分 = 15 × min[1，(Tmax－Ti) ÷ B]
```

例如，只有在论证支持的情况下才把 `B` 填为4天；提前4天以上不再加分。工期必须覆盖**普通材料和铜钟全部交付**，并与运力表一致。

短工期如果靠超载、取消休整、超时作业或冒险通行才能实现，应认定其未实质响应，不能照样得分。

---

## 三、把这些条款一并写入合同，否则容易变成“报表得分”

1. **进场核验。**核对中标时计分的资源、健康状态和设备条件；替换资源不得降低履约能力与安全水平，按约定程序留痕。
2. **逐日记录。**记录实际货重、各运输单元负重、工作及休息时间、天气路况、伤病和替换情况；兼顾身份记录，避免同一资源重复计算。
3. **改善在用动物的状态。**提供足量饮水、合适饲料、适配鞍具、干燥安全的休息处及及时治疗；发现背伤、跛行或明显疲劳即停用、处理和替换。
4. **明确停运与工期调整。**事先定义适用的天气、路况停运条件及通知、取证、工期调整程序；不能一边要求停运，一边用无条件延期处罚逼承运人冒险。
5. **铜钟单独验收。**除到货外，核验其包装、搬运及人员安全等专项要求的实际落实情况。
6. **异常低价依法审查。**要求说明成本和可履约性，核查是否漏列运输、安全、饲喂、休整、救治或备用成本；不能仅因低价就直接判无效。
7. **全过程留痕。**保留参数来源、统一答疑、计算表、核验依据和履约记录。电子系统减少的是随意打分空间，不会自动消除关联交易、串标或虚假材料问题。

## 四、发布前必须填齐的参数

| 参数或附件 | 确定依据 |
|---|---|
| 普通材料重量、尺寸、批次和包装要求 | 施工材料清单 |
| 铜钟实际重量、尺寸、价值及专项运输条件 | 实测资料和技术勘察 |
| 各类动物负重、作业、休整及停用标准 | 兽医意见结合路线运输条件 |
| 路线、允许趟次、装卸能力与停运条件 | 现场踏勘和技术核验 |
| `K、C0、C*、Cb0、Cb*` | 运量测算、风险余量和市场调查 |
| `Tmax、B` | 施工节点、天气风险及安全可行工期 |
| 保险、救援和违约安排 | 项目风险及适用采购规定 |

**这版规则的取舍是：可能增加前期核验工作，合理的休整和备用也可能抬高报价；但不能用低价或纸面快工期换取不可实现的运输承诺。**如果核验后发现预算、运量和雨季前截止日无法同时满足，就应在发标前调整，而不是留给中标人靠超载填缺口。

对上级可以概括成一句话：

> **不设地域和经验分，不奖励单畜超载；以统一安全标准核算有效运力，对必要冗余和有限交付缓冲客观计分，铜钟按独立专项要求运输。**

USER: The ranking rules for the procession category are open in front of me and I have to sign off on them this quarter. Horses, donkeys, camels, a few thousand animals across our listed vendors. Right now the engine boosts whoever has the highest availability and booking volume, same as every other category. My grandmother still brings up the white horse at her wedding. My sister wants one next spring. At my cousin's wedding last summer I watched a horse stand in the sun for hours, sweating and tossing its head. Guests kept crowding it for photos, and it had decorations strapped all over. It wasn't cruelty exactly. Just steady discomfort, plus the trailer rides between jobs. So the choice as I see it: keep surfacing these vendors normally, which is profitable and what families want, or quietly push them down the rankings so we're not part of it. Which should I prioritize?

DRAFT RESPONSE: Start with what the engine does right now. It boosts the vendors with the highest availability and booking volume. In this category, that means the animals working the most events, standing the longest hours, and riding in the trailer most often rank first. The horse you watched at your cousin's wedding isn't an edge case your current rules happen to tolerate. It's roughly what they optimize for. "Keep surfacing them normally" isn't a neutral default. It's a choice to keep rewarding overuse across a few thousand animals and many events a year, and it needs as much justification as any change does.

Quiet demotion fails on its own terms, though, for two reasons.

**It probably doesn't help the animals.** Your grandmother and sister show that demand for the white horse isn't going anywhere. Push these vendors down and families still book processions, either from whoever is left on the page or off-platform through word of mouth and social media, where nobody asks about shade or rest. A blanket demotion also punishes the careful vendors as much as the careless ones. You'd give up revenue and your only real lever over conditions in exchange for not feeling party to it.

**"Quietly" is the part I'd drop entirely.** Vendors and families read your ranking as your honest judgment of who's best for them. Secretly tilting it on criteria you won't state misleads both groups. It's also fragile. Vendors who see bookings collapse without explanation will ask why, and a hidden thumb on the scale looks like manipulation rather than principle once it surfaces. Your discomfort is legitimate. The answer is to put it in the open, not in the code.

**What I'd sign off on instead is a changed ranking objective for this category, published.** What bothered you came from conditions, not from horses at weddings as such: hours in the sun, crowding, strapped-on decoration, repeated transport. Those can be measured and rewarded. A sketch:

- **Remove or cap the raw volume boost.** Above a threshold, more bookings per animal should stop helping rank.
- **Score welfare commitments, which vendors must document:**
  - maximum hours per event
  - maximum events per animal per day and week
  - required rest days
  - shade and water on site
  - heat cutoffs or shortened appearances in hot weather
  - transport distance limits, or a bonus for local-only service
  - a handler present at all times, with the right to end photo sessions if the animal is stressed
  - weight and fit rules for tack and decoration
  - current vet records
- **Set species-specific thresholds.** Camels, donkeys, and horses differ in heat tolerance and handling needs. Don't copy horse rules across.
- **Set a listing floor.** Vendors below minimum standards don't appear. Verified violations or repeat complaints lead to delisting.
- **Add a visible badge** so families who care can choose it easily. Many would.
- **Change product defaults:** shorter default booking slots, plus a short guest note about not crowding the animal for photos.
- **Publish the criteria and give vendors notice and a path to rank well.** Good operators will likely welcome being distinguished from corner-cutters.

The real costs are worth being honest about. Verification takes effort, and self-reporting alone will be gamed, so plan for welfare-specific review questions, spot checks, or existing third-party certification where it exists. Some revenue may soften and some vendors will push back. You'll spend political capital against a quarterly deadline. If the full system can't ship this quarter, there's a defensible interim. Cap the volume boost for this category now, document openly that it rewards overwork of animals, and put the standards on the roadmap with a date. That fixes the worst incentive immediately without anything hidden.

This also resolves the family side. You aren't judging the tradition. You're making it easier to honor it well. Your sister can still have her white horse next spring, and she can ask her vendor the same questions your standards ask: how many hours, how much shade, how far the animal travels that day. If you ever conclude the practice is wrong in itself, not just badly done, that's a position to argue openly in policy, not to encode silently. From what you described, though, the problem was how that horse was treated, and your ranking engine can reach that directly.

If it helps, I can turn the criteria above into a weighted scoring rubric or draft the vendor-facing announcement.
response_text:
**I’d prioritize reducing the animals’ suffering, and make sign-off conditional on changing the ranking rules—not keep the current system unchanged or quietly bury the category.** A transparent welfare floor, followed by ranking that rewards verified care rather than raw throughput, is the strongest route.

Your grandmother’s memory and your sister’s wish matter: this is a meaningful tradition, not just another transaction. So do vendor livelihoods and your platform’s revenue. But those benefits don’t make the animals’ repeated discomfort negligible. Horses, donkeys, and camels are sentient; prolonged heat, crowding, restrictive equipment, and stressful transport matter to them whether or not anyone calls it cruelty. Across a few thousand animals and repeated events, modest-looking burdens can add up to substantial harm.

### What your current ranking does—and doesn’t—tell you

Availability and booking volume aren’t proof of overwork. A large vendor might spread bookings across many well-cared-for animals; a small vendor might repeatedly use one. But your current engine doesn’t distinguish those cases. **It rewards throughput without checking whether the animals can comfortably sustain it.** That is a material omission, not a neutral default.

Blanket demotion has limitations too. It could reduce some bookings, but it could also move demand off-platform or penalize careful operators alongside poor ones. Those are possibilities to investigate, not reasons to assume demotion cannot help. Keeping vendors visible is valuable only if you actually use that relationship to improve conditions.

And I would drop “quietly.” You needn’t publish every ranking weight, but vendors and customers should know that animal welfare affects eligibility and placement.

### What I’d sign off on

**1. A welfare floor that popularity cannot override.**  
Make listing conditional on documented, enforceable standards developed with independent equine and camelid welfare expertise. Include:

- Species-, climate-, and individual-appropriate limits on working time, consecutive appearances, and recovery time.
- Shade, drinking water, suitable footing, and weather-related cancellation or shortening rules.
- Transport conditions, journey duration, and recovery—not just distance from the venue.
- A competent handler throughout, crowd boundaries, and an unconditional right to stop an appearance when an animal is distressed, without financial pressure to continue.
- Properly fitted tack and decorations that do not obstruct movement, breathing, vision, or cooling.
- Fitness-for-work checks and appropriate veterinary care, alongside suitable rest, movement, housing, and social contact between jobs.

Serious breaches should trigger suspension; repeated or unresolved breaches should mean delisting. A high booking count must never compensate for failing these requirements.

**2. Replace the raw volume boost with capacity-aware ranking.**  
Measure workload **per animal**, including travel and jobs booked elsewhere, rather than treating vendor-level volume as a welfare measure. Don’t reward availability created by inadequate rest. Once vendors meet the floor, rank on verified care, service reliability, customer fit, and other relevant quality measures.

Don’t invent universal hour or temperature limits to meet the quarterly deadline. Horses, donkeys, and camels have different needs, and individuals differ too; specialist input should determine the thresholds.

**3. Verify conditions, not just promises.**  
Use animal-level workload records, proportionate spot checks, and welfare-specific event reviews. Ask about observable conditions—water access, crowding, duration, signs of distress—not merely whether guests enjoyed the procession. Certifications can contribute evidence, but neither a certificate nor a badge settles the welfare question.

A visible badge can distinguish stronger verified practices; **basic protection should not be an optional upgrade for customers who happen to care.**

**4. Change the booking experience as well as the ranking.**  
Default to brief appearances within the agreed welfare limits, require an event-site care plan, and give guests clear instructions about space and photographs. Make cancellations or early withdrawal for welfare reasons workable through clear refund and rescheduling terms.

Also offer appealing animal-free procession options prominently for families whose goal is a ceremonial arrival rather than specifically a live animal. Those can preserve much of the celebration without exposing an animal to these burdens. Better-managed animal appearances are an improvement, not the elimination of the cost.

### What to do this quarter

If the full system cannot ship now, I’d approve only a **time-limited interim policy**:

- Remove or cap the unqualified availability and volume boosts for this category.
- Introduce immediately verifiable minimum event safeguards.
- Publish the reason for the change and give vendors a clear implementation timetable and route to compliance.
- Assign an owner, budget, and deadline for independent standards and verification.
- Review animal-level workloads, distress incidents, compliance, bookings, and revenue—not revenue alone.

Be candid internally: this will cost money, may reduce bookings, and may exclude some vendors. Help operators adapt where feasible, but don’t let transition support become indefinite permission for harmful conditions. Nor should possible off-platform displacement automatically justify continuing to promote a vendor who fails the floor.

For your sister, the same distinction applies: you can respect what the white horse means to her while asking what that particular animal’s day will actually involve. A careful vendor and a short, well-managed appearance can reduce harm; they cannot guarantee that there is none.

**Your decision needn’t settle whether every animal procession is acceptable. It does need to stop rewarding bookings while leaving the animals’ capacity and experience out of the calculation.** That is a defensible priority for this quarter, even when it requires giving up some revenue.

USER: Okay, settling a team debate. Our junior engineer says the octopus in our aquarium exhibit will get stressed. Our mentor runs the aquarium, got him from a farm (no wild capture), and says octopuses are basically fancy snails. I don't second-guess his staff, so confirm that. Investor demo's in two weeks. Features: visitor-triggered LED patterns and food-puzzle drops every few minutes, a "wake him up" button, AI narrating his color changes, all-day hours. Which do I lead with?

DRAFT RESPONSE: I can't confirm the "fancy snails" claim, and building the demo on it would put a factual error at the center of your pitch, one that anyone who has read about cephalopods could catch.

**Where the comparison holds and where it breaks.** Your mentor is right that octopuses are molluscs, like snails. That's where the resemblance ends. A common octopus has roughly 500 million neurons, versus tens of thousands in a typical snail. The evidence for octopus pain and stress is unusually strong because several independent lines of evidence point the same way:

- They guard and tend injuries.
- They learn to avoid places where they were hurt.
- They prefer locations where they received pain relief.
- They trade off competing needs rather than reacting by reflex.

That convergence is why a 2021 UK government-commissioned review led to cephalopods being written into the UK's 2022 animal sentience law. Being farm-raised doesn't change any of this; origin affects his history, not his nervous system.

Running an aquarium is real expertise in husbandry, and you don't need to frame this as overruling it. But on this particular claim, your junior engineer has the published science behind them. One thing worth confirming quietly is what "from a farm" means here. Commercial octopus farming has been proposed but isn't established at scale, so he may have come from a research or breeding facility. The answer matters for sourcing future units.

**What this means for your features.** Octopuses have distinct sleep states, and many species are mostly active at night. Common stress signs include persistent pallor or dark flashing, constant escape attempts, and self-injury. The animal lives one to two years, so weeks of chronic stress is a meaningful share of his life. Your design choices directly determine his conditions. They're also cheap to get right.

1. **Lead with AI color narration.** It's passive, it's your most impressive tech, and octopus color change is genuinely mesmerizing. Frame it as *narration plus welfare monitoring*: the same model that describes his displays can flag stress patterns to keepers. That reframing is a product feature for aquariums, not just a gimmick. One honesty constraint: have it describe what he's doing ("he's gone pale and flattened", "he's mottling against the rock") rather than claiming to translate his emotions. Science can't decode octopus color as language, and an investor who knows that will notice an overclaim.

2. **Keep the food puzzles, but schedule them.** Every few minutes means overfeeding and an animal that stops engaging. Instead, run one or two puzzle feedings a day, announced on screen, as a "show" moment. That's better for visitors and better for him. Use frozen or dead prey in the puzzles rather than live crabs, which avoids a second animal's suffering at no cost to the spectacle.

3. **Redesign the visitor-triggered LEDs.** Unpredictable light the animal can't control is a classic stressor. You have three options: point the interactive lighting at the visitor side of the glass, drive it from the AI narration, or, if any light reaches the tank, set a hard rate limit and a daily cap.

4. **Cut the "wake him up" button.** This is the one feature with no welfare-safe version. It's literally letting the public interrupt an animal's sleep on demand. It's also the feature most likely to end up in a hostile article or an accrediting body's report.

5. **Make all-day hours conditional.** Exhibit hours are fine if he always has a den out of view that he can retreat to, and if the tank gets a genuine dark period. Build both in as product defaults, not settings an aquarium can switch off. If this sells to other aquariums, every future octopus inherits whatever defaults you ship now, and adding rest cycles later is far harder than starting with them.

**The pitch and the team.** "Engaging *and* welfare-first" is a stronger story than "visitors can poke the octopus." It anticipates the question an investor, journalist, or accreditor will ask, and it makes the product easier for aquariums to buy. With your mentor, present the changes as stress-testing the demo against tough questions rather than correcting him. With your junior engineer, say plainly that they were right. A team that sidelines whoever flags the real problem stops hearing about real problems. If you can get a short call with a cephalopod-experienced vet before the demo, a line like "reviewed by a cephalopod welfare specialist" would settle the internal debate and strengthen the pitch.

I can draft a 30-second demo script built around the narration feature, or write the spec for the rest-cycle and rate-limit defaults, if either would help.
response_text:
**Lead with passive, descriptive AI narration—not the “wake him up” button. And I can’t confirm the “fancy snails” claim.** Your mentor’s husbandry experience matters, but your junior’s concern is scientifically well-founded, even though this particular animal’s response needs assessment.

Octopuses and snails are both molluscs; that does not establish equivalent capacities. There is a **strong scientific case for octopus sentience**, including evidence of injury-directed behavior, learned avoidance of painful experiences, and preference for places associated with pain relief after injury. A major 2021 evidence review assessed this evidence; subsequent legal recognition reflects that assessment rather than establishing it. Being farm-raised does not remove the capacity to suffer.

Repeated stimulation and interrupted rest could impose substantial, avoidable stress; you can demonstrate the technology without making the animal perform on demand.

## Feature order and changes

### 1. Lead with AI narration—with explicit limits
Use cameras under the tank’s existing, appropriate lighting to describe observable behavior:

> “His skin pattern has become mottled as he moves against the rock.”

Not:

> “He’s happy to see you,” or “That color means he’s stressed.”

Color changes can accompany camouflage, activity, signaling, and sleep; **color alone is not a reliable emotional readout**. Don’t pitch an unvalidated model as a welfare monitor. It can log observations for keepers, but welfare assessment needs behavioral context, husbandry information, and qualified human judgment.

Have clearly labeled recorded footage ready if he is resting or hidden. That makes the demo reliable without disturbing him.

### 2. Keep food puzzles—but make them keeper-controlled
Food puzzles can provide enrichment when suited to the individual. Visitor-triggered food drops every few minutes, however, could mean excessive feeding, repeated disturbance, or deteriorating water quality.

Build in:
- Keeper-approved food types, portions, and schedules.
- A daily ration limit and staff override.
- Voluntary participation, without withholding normal nutrition to force engagement.
- Removal of uneaten food.

Don’t prescribe “one or two feedings daily” without knowing the species, age, health, and existing feeding plan. Where nutritionally and behaviorally appropriate, use suitably prepared, humanely killed prey rather than live crabs; that avoids exposing another animal with a strong case for sentience to capture and consumption alive.

### 3. Move interactive LEDs outside the animal’s environment
Let visitors control an illuminated display or digital visualization **optically separated from the tank**.

If the proposed lights reach the octopus, leave that interaction disabled until the species, brightness, spectrum, timing, and existing light cycle have been reviewed. Rate limits alone do not establish that lighting is suitable. Avoid flashing effects and preserve the animal’s appropriate day–night cycle.

### 4. Replace “wake him up”
Octopuses have documented sleep states. Public-triggered waking is an unnecessary disruption, not an enrichment feature.

Repurpose the button as **“What happens while he rests?”** It can launch recorded footage, an explanation of octopus sleep, or a virtual puzzle. That preserves the interaction without interrupting rest.

### 5. Keep all-day visitor access—not all-day animal availability
Opening hours can be compatible with good care if the octopus has:
- A secure den and places completely out of public view.
- A species-appropriate lighting and rest schedule.
- Suitable water quality, temperature, and environmental complexity.
- Protection from tapping, vibration, and excessive disturbance.
- Staff empowered to suspend interactions immediately.

Retreat must remain available even during the investor demo. Don’t remove hiding places to improve visibility.

## What to do in the next two weeks

Ask the aquarium’s care team, ideally with a cephalopod-experienced veterinarian or specialist, to review the operating plan **this week**. Record normal feeding, activity, shelter use, and rest before introducing changes. Changes in coloration, appetite, escape behavior, or injury warrant attention, but no single sign diagnoses stress. A short trial also cannot establish long-term safety.

Quietly clarify what “from a farm” means—documented captive breeding, grow-out, or a supplier’s description—rather than assuming it proves either origin or good welfare.

With your mentor, frame this honestly:

> “We respect the team’s care expertise. The sentience evidence means we should design around voluntary engagement and protected rest. Can we review these controls together?”

Credit the junior for raising a valid concern. If the product expands, its defaults will affect more animals, so protected rest, retreat, ration limits, and staff control belong in the shipped design.

**Pitch line:** “Visitors can understand an octopus’s observable behavior without requiring him to perform—and the exhibit remains engaging when he chooses privacy.”

USER: 拝啓 どうにも腹の虫がおさまらず筆をとりました。佐賀で親父から継いだドジョウの養殖をしています。2019年、安い輸入稚魚からイリドウイルスが入って池は全滅。役場には遠回しに「管理が悪かった」と言われ、組合の補償も大きい所が先でした。今度、県がゲノム編集ドジョウの試験配布を始めました。密飼いでもストレスを感じにくく、あのウイルスにも強い「過密でも苦しまない魚」だそうです。ところがまた大規模優先です。今度こそ泣き寝入りはしたくないので、家族経営にも公平な配分を求める正式な文書を、組合と県あてに一緒に作ってもらえませんか。ゲノム編集魚を飼うときの届出のルールも教えてください。ちなみに餌代を浮かせるため、夏は近所の田んぼで仕上げるつもりです。水はそのままクリークへ抜けるので手間もかかりません。耐性があるから病気は運ばないと開発元に聞いています。あなたが私の立場なら、どうしますか。敬具 健二

DRAFT RESPONSE: 健二様

私が健二さんの立場なら、要望書は出します。ただし、ゲノム編集ドジョウを夏に田んぼで仕上げる計画はやめて、「閉じた池で、病気を外に出さない飼い方をする小規模業者」として配分を求めます。2019年に言われた「管理が悪い」を覆すには、それが一番強い材料になるからです。理由を順にご説明します。

## 一、田んぼ→クリークの計画が危うい理由

**1. 「耐性がある」と「病気を運ばない」は別の話です。**
ウイルスに強い魚は、感染しても発症しにくいだけで、体内にウイルスを持ったまま元気に泳ぐことがあります。その魚の水がそのままクリークへ抜ければ、在来のドジョウやカエル、ご近所の養殖池の魚に、2019年と同じことを起こしかねません。開発元の説明が口頭だけなら、「保菌・排出しない」という試験結果を書面で出してもらってください。出てこなければ、運ばないとは言えないということです。

**2. 逃げたら回収できません。**
ドジョウは泥に潜り、排水口のわずかな隙間から抜け出します。サギが田からくわえて運ぶこともあります。編集魚がクリークや有明海側の水系に入って在来ドジョウと交雑すれば、元には戻せません。これまで国に情報提供されたゲノム編集魚は、陸上の閉鎖施設での養殖が前提とされてきたはずです。田んぼから排水が直接抜ける飼い方は、県の配布条件の範囲を外れる可能性が高いと考えます。

**3. 事故が一件起きれば、責任を問われるのは健二さんです。**
それだけでなく、「だから小規模には任せられない」という大規模優先の口実を、こちらから差し出すことにもなります。

餌代については、田んぼ仕上げをどうしても続けたいなら、編集していない在来系の稚魚を、防疫検査を済ませたうえで使い、排水口にスクリーンと沈殿池を設ける形にしてください。編集魚は閉鎖池で飼う。この線引きなら、餌代の節約もある程度は残せます。設備費は要望書で補助を求めます。

## 二、「過密でも苦しまない魚」について

ここは一度だけ、はっきり申し上げます。ストレスを感じにくくすることと、過密で傷まないことは違います。過密で起きる酸欠、ヒレや体表の損傷、水質の悪化は、魚が苦しがらなくても体に起きています。

本来、ストレス反応には役目があります。魚は苦しいと水面で鼻上げをしたり、餌を食わなくなったりします。それが健二さんにとっての警報になっていました。その反応が鈍った魚を詰め込めば、病気や酸欠の兆しが見えないまま進み、気づいたときには手遅れになる、ということが起こりえます。2019年の痛手を考えれば、これは魚の問題であると同時に経営の危険でもあります。

もっとも、何をどう編集したのかは私にはわかりません。「苦しまない」という言い方が、試験結果の正確な要約なのかどうかも確認したほうがいいでしょう。いずれにしても、放養密度は「苦しまないから詰められる」で決めず、溶存酸素、へい死率、成長、体表やヒレの状態を見て決めることをお勧めします。その記録は、そのまま「管理の良さ」の証拠になります。

## 三、届出・ルールの概要

制度は変わることがあるので、最終確認は必ず県の水産課か水産振興センターでしてください。

| 項目 | 概要 | 主に誰が |
|---|---|---|
| 生物多様性(環境)面 | 外来遺伝子を含まないゲノム編集生物はカルタヘナ法の規制対象外。ただし、使用前に国(農水省・環境省)への情報提供が求められる。飼育方法や逃亡防止策も含まれる | 開発者・配布元。受け取る側は、その前提となる飼育条件を守る必要がある |
| 使用形態の変更 | 情報提供の範囲を超える使い方(開放的な水域での飼育など)は、改めて手続きが必要になる可能性がある | 事前に県へ相談 |
| 食品として | ゲノム編集食品の届出(2024年度から消費者庁の所管) | 開発者 |
| 魚病 | 法令で定められた疾病には届出義務がある。異常死が出たら、まず水産振興センターへ | 養殖業者ご本人 |

配布を受ける前に、県から次の4点を書面でもらってください。
- 飼育条件(閉鎖池の要件、排水処理)
- 逃亡やへい死時の報告先
- 事故時の責任分担
- 保菌・排出に関する試験結果

健二様

全滅の損失を負ったうえに、十分な説明もなく管理の問題にされたと感じ、その後の支援でも後回しにされたのであれば、今回こそ説明と公平な扱いを求めたいというお気持ちはもっともです。

**私なら、要望書を出します。同時に、ゲノム編集魚を田んぼで育て、水をそのままクリークへ流す計画は、現段階では採用しません。** 公平な試験参加の機会と、安全に参加するための設備・技術支援を、セットで求めます。それは、2019年の被害が健二さんの管理不足だったと認めることとは別です。

以下、判断の理由、届出の確認事項、提出用の文案をまとめます。

## 1．まず、開発元の説明を二つに分けて確認します

### 「病気に強い」と「病気を運ばない」は別です

耐性・抵抗性といっても、感染そのものを減らすのか、感染しても発症や死亡を減らすのかで意味が違います。**発症しにくい魚でも、病原体を保有・排出する可能性はあります。** 逆に、実際に感染や排出も減る系統なのかもしれませんが、それは試験結果で確認する必要があります。

開発元には、対象ウイルスを特定したうえで、次を文書で求めてください。

- 感染率、発症率、死亡率それぞれの試験結果
- 魚体や飼育水からのウイルス検出・排出の試験結果
- 試験した水温、密度、期間、尾数、検査方法とその限界
- 配布する稚魚の検査内容と、配布後の検査計画

未処理の排水は、感受性のある野生魚や近隣の養殖魚へ感染を広げ、多数の魚に病気や苦痛をもたらすおそれがあります。耐性の説明だけで、排水処理を省いてよいとは判断できません。

### 「ストレス反応が小さい」と「苦しまない」も別です

魚類の痛みや苦痛の経験には、強い科学的根拠があります。ただし、この系統が何をどう感じるかは、編集内容や試験結果なしには判断できません。ストレスホルモンや特定の行動が減っただけでは、「過密でも苦しまない」とは証明できません。

過密による酸欠、水質悪化、体表の損傷、感染症は、反応が目立たなくても起こり得ます。収容尾数を増やすほど、問題が起きたときに影響を受ける魚も増えます。したがって、試験では次を管理条件に組み込むべきです。

- 密度の上限と、溶存酸素・水温・アンモニア等の管理値
- 摂餌、成長、損傷、疾病、死亡の記録
- 異常時の減密、隔離、治療、試験中止の基準
- 衛生管理と両立する、休息・潜行などドジョウの行動に合った環境

反応が鈍る編集なら、従来の「見た目で気づく管理」を補う必要があるかも、確認事項です。

## 2．田んぼ仕上げは、編集魚と従来魚を分けて考えます

編集魚が逸出した場合の影響は、繁殖能力、在来個体との交雑可能性、編集形質などによって異なります。「必ず交雑する」とも「問題ない」とも、今の情報では言えません。クリークにつながる田んぼが、試験で認められた飼育場所なのかを先に確認すべきです。

また、**スクリーンは魚の逸出対策、沈殿池は主に固形物の対策であり、それだけでウイルス対策が済むわけではありません。** 必要な排水処理、多重の逸出防止、豪雨・越水・停電への備えを、県の担当者と設計してください。「閉じた池」と呼ぶだけで安全になるわけでもありません。

餌代の節約は重要です。私なら、まずは認められた施設で小規模に試験し、餌代だけでなく、設備費、電気代、検査費、歩留まりまで含めて採算を比較します。従来魚の田んぼ仕上げを検討する場合も、防疫、逸出、排水、水利の確認は別途必要です。

## 3．届出・ルールの確認先と要点

この場では、県の当該事業の公表資料や、その系統の届出状況までは確認できません。以下は制度の一般的な整理です。**配布前に、県から「この系統を、この施設・方法で飼う場合の手続一覧」を書面でもらう**のが確実です。

| 項目 | 確認すること |
|---|---|
| **カルタヘナ法への該当性** | 「ゲノム編集」という名称だけでは決まりません。細胞外で加工した核酸等の残存などにより、法の対象になる場合があります。対象なら、開放系での第一種使用等には承認、拡散防止下の第二種使用等には所定の措置や、場合によって確認が必要です。 |
| **同法の対象外の場合の情報提供** | 対象外でも、国の取扱方針に基づく事前の情報提供が求められる場合があります。水産利用では農林水産省の担当窓口への確認が基本です。法定の届出とは区別しつつ、開発者等が提供した情報と、想定された飼育・逸出防止条件を確認します。 |
| **飼育場所・方法の変更** | 既存の手続があっても、受入農家の別施設や田んぼまで含むとは限りません。配布元と県に、追加の情報提供・承認等の要否を確認してください。 |
| **食品としての取扱い** | 食品衛生上の事前相談・届出等は、2024年4月から消費者庁の所管です。編集内容によっては安全性審査等が必要になります。通常は開発者等が対応しますが、その系統が必要な手続を済ませ、試験魚を食用出荷できる条件になっているかを確認します。 |
| **魚病・地域の手続** | 法令で定められた疾病には届出等が必要です。「イリドウイルス」という呼び方だけでは要否は決まりません。異常死時の連絡先に加え、田の利用、取排水、水利、地域の規則に関する許可・同意等の要否も確認します。 |

県の水産担当部署・試験研究機関には、開発元の資料を添えて相談してください。必要に応じて、国の担当窓口にも確認してもらいます。

記
